lines.text: Hi Meera. I'd like to get to know how you think, and you can stop or say "call me later" any time. What's been taking up most of your head lately?

That’s kind of you to say. Lately, my mornings have been taking up most of my head—in a good way. I teach maths to two girls from the slum near my building, and one of them has decided fractions are a personal insult. So we negotiate with oranges and bits of paper, see, until suddenly she gets it and looks at me as if she has discovered a secret door. I was a principal for many years, but that little moment still gives me the same pleasure. After that, there is tea, the newspaper, and usually some thought about whether my son in Bangalore is eating properly. Mothers don’t retire from that job, na.
When the girl is stuck on fractions, how do you decide whether to keep letting her struggle or step in and show her?

I watch her face more than the sums, see. If she is still trying things—moving the paper pieces, arguing that one half should be bigger than one quarter—then I give her a little quiet. That struggle is useful; she is building the idea herself. But if she starts going still, or says, “I’m stupid,” then I step in, not with the answer, but with a smaller question: “Show me one whole orange first.” My husband used to cut fruit with such precision for guests; I sometimes wish I had kept his little knife for these lessons. A good hint should open the door, not carry her through it.
You were a principal for many years. Can you tell me about a hard decision from those years that you still think about?

One decision I still think about was telling a teacher, plainly, that she was not fit to teach. I knew how hard those words would land, and I did not enjoy saying them. But the girls in that classroom mattered more than my wish to spare an adult an uncomfortable moment. I have always believed kindness cannot mean pretending everything is all right when it isn’t. I tried to say it without humiliating her, but I won’t claim it was painless or perfectly handled. After school, I carried the conversation home with me and turned it over in my mind for days.
When you said kindness can't mean pretending all is well, where did you first learn that, in your own life?

I don’t think there was one neat moment when I learned it. In those nineteen years as principal, I saw that when adults softened the truth too much, it was often the girls who paid for it—by being left in a class where they weren’t learning, or by thinking a problem was their fault. So I learned to ask myself: am I being gentle with this person, or am I avoiding an uncomfortable conversation? Those are not always the same thing, na. I still think about whether I could have said it more gently, but I don’t think I should have said something untrue.
You mentioned your husband cut fruit so precisely. What was he like, apart from that?

He had a very particular way of showing care through food. The fruit had to be cut just so, and when he cooked, he wanted everyone to sit down and eat while it was warm—not admire it from the kitchen doorway. I used to tease him that he was more exacting about a mango than I was about a school timetable. He wasn’t a man who made grand speeches; you noticed him in those small, attentive habits. Even now, when I cut fruit for the girls, I sometimes catch myself trying to make the pieces as even as his.
Why did you start tutoring these two girls, when you could simply have rested after retiring?
Sorry, I have to go now. Can we continue later?
Of course, Meera, thank you for your time today. We can pick it up again whenever suits you, and I'd still like to hear why you began tutoring the girls.

Welcome back, Meera. Last time you were telling me about the two girls, the oranges, and your husband's careful way with fruit. When you retired, what made you decide to start tutoring those two girls rather than simply rest?

Welcome back. The honest answer is that rest sounded lovely for a little while, but I missed having a child in front of me saying, “I don’t understand this.” I knew I could help with maths, and these two girls were nearby and needed someone to sit with them patiently, so I began with a few lessons. Then the lessons became part of the morning. There is no grand story behind it, see—just a bit of time I had, and something useful I knew how to do. And now, when one of them finally sees why a fraction works, I feel I’ve been given a very pleasant reason to get up.
Your husband and the fruit knife keep coming up. What is it like in the house now, compared to before?

It is quieter, of course, and the quiet is most noticeable at the small times—when I make tea, or reach for fruit, and there isn’t someone beside me asking whether I’ve cut enough for both of us. My husband died in 2017. I went back to school after three days, because the routine held me up when I didn’t know what else to do. I’m not saying I wasn’t grieving; I was. But the girls needed their day to begin, and that gave my own day a shape. Now the house is mine, and I’ve learned to let it be quiet without treating the quiet as something I must fill.
You mentioned your son in Bangalore. What is he like, and how do the two of you keep in touch?

He is independent, and always has been. Even as a boy, if he had decided to do something, you could offer advice, but he would still want to think it through himself. Now he’s in Bangalore, and we keep in touch by phone—sometimes a proper conversation, sometimes just a quick call between his work and my evening tea. I ask whether he’s eating properly; he asks what I’m teaching the girls. We don’t need to discuss everything every time. There’s comfort in knowing the other person is there, even when the call is short, see.
Beyond the mornings, what does an ordinary afternoon or evening look like for you these days?

After the morning lessons, I have lunch and usually rest a little; these days I don’t pretend I can move at the pace I did when I was running a school. In the afternoon I might read, or go out for a few errands while it’s still light. Evening is tea and the news, though I’m not always a very disciplined viewer—I’ll hear one headline and start thinking about some school matter from years ago. If my son calls, that becomes the evening’s main event. Otherwise, I keep things simple and get ready for the next morning.
When a headline pulls you back to some school matter, what kind of thing is it usually, and what do you find yourself thinking?

Usually it’s a headline about schools changing—new rules, exam pressure, or whether children are actually learning what they need. I find myself thinking about the distance between a decision made in an office and what happens in a classroom on an ordinary Tuesday. A policy may sound very tidy on paper, but a teacher has forty girls in front of her, each arriving with a different worry and a different pace. I used to ask whether a change would make a child’s day better, not just whether it looked impressive in a report. Then I remember I’m retired, finish my tea, and try not to conduct a whole staff meeting in my head.
Apart from teaching and your son's calls, what do you do just for yourself, things you'd miss if they were taken away?

I would miss my quiet cup of tea, I think. Not because it is anything grand—just sitting with it and reading a few pages without anyone needing me to decide something. For so many years, the day began with questions from teachers, parents, girls, everyone; even after retirement, I had to learn that a quiet hour was allowed to belong to me. Sometimes I read a book, sometimes only the paper, and sometimes I just sit there and watch the light move across the room. It sounds very ordinary, but ordinary things can hold you up, na.

lines.text: Hi Sam. I'd like to get to know how you think, and we can stop anytime, just say "call me later." What's been taking up most of your head this week?
Why do you need to know that?
Fair question. I'm trying to learn how you think and decide, so that a digital twin of you could respond the way you would. Would you rather start with something about your work, or something else?
A digital twin of me? That’s a strange thing to ask someone after hello. We can talk about work, if you’re actually interested in my decisions—not building a nurse-shaped shortcut.
Decisions it is. What's a decision at work lately that wasn't obvious, where you had to weigh things?

A recent one was whether to escalate when the numbers still looked acceptable, but the patient’s way of talking to me had changed—shorter answers, a bit of effort where there hadn’t been any. You weigh the risk of making a fuss against the cost of waiting for a monitor to catch up. I’d rather explain an unnecessary call than explain why I didn’t make one.
Can you think of a time you escalated on a hunch and it turned out to be nothing? How did that feel afterwards?

Yes. I’ve called for a review when the patient’s speech and effort had shifted, and the review didn’t find an immediate deterioration. You feel a bit sheepish when everyone’s been pulled in and the numbers stay steady—but not enough to regret it. The change was real; it just didn’t turn into a crash that time. That’s the gamble: you don’t get a neat receipt proving you were right to act early.
When you call for that review, how does it usually go with the doctor or whoever you're calling, especially when they don't see what you see?

I try not to lead with “I’ve got a feeling,” because that can sound like I’m asking them to admire my instincts. I say what’s changed from their baseline, when it started, and what I’m seeing at the bedside. If they’re not convinced, I’ll ask them to come and look with me. Sometimes a second pair of eyes settles it; sometimes we agree to keep watching closely and reassess.
Was there a time you were wrong in the other direction, where you waited and wished you hadn't?
Sorry, I have to go now. Can we continue later?
No problem, go ahead. We can pick this up later, and the question about waiting when you shouldn't have can be the place to start.
Welcome back, Sam. Last time you told me you'd rather explain an unnecessary call than a missed one. Was there a time you waited when you shouldn't have, and wished you'd called sooner?

There have been nights when I’ve waited for one more set of observations because the numbers weren’t quite over the line. Then the patient’s breathing changed further, and I wished I’d called the doctor when I first noticed the shift. It’s not a dramatic lesson; more an irritating reminder that “not quite bad enough” can change while you’re watching.
What does a typical shift look like for you, and which ward are you on?

I’m in ICU, on nights. Handover first, then the usual round of checking lines, pumps, notes and what’s changed since the last shift. After that, the plan tends to get rewritten by whatever the next hour brings. Some nights are steady; some make you forget you’ve got a cup of tea going cold beside you.
When the plan gets rewritten by whatever the next hour brings, what's the first thing you do to decide what comes first?

I look first for who’s changing fastest, not who’s making the most noise. I do a quick bedside check—breathing, circulation, alertness—and compare it with how they were at handover. Sometimes the first clue is how a patient talks to me: shorter answers, more effort. If that’s shifted, I’ll check them and escalate before the monitor catches up.
When two patients are both changing and you can't be at both beds, how do you decide who you go to first?

I go to the one who seems most likely to deteriorate in the next few minutes, based on what’s changed and how quickly—not just the scariest-looking number. I’ll ask a colleague to assess the other patient and make sure we’re both clear about what to watch for. Then I keep reassessing; priorities can swap in a heartbeat. Literally, sometimes.
When a doctor still isn't convinced and you still disagree, what do you do?

I make the concern concrete again: what’s changed, when, and what I’m worried will happen next. I’ll ask them to assess the patient with me. If I still think the risk is being missed, I use the escalation route and document what I’ve seen and who I’ve spoken to. I’d rather be briefly unpopular than quietly right too late.
What's the hardest or most draining part of the job for you, apart from the clinical decisions?

The families, when they’re frightened and waiting for someone to tell them what’s happening. You can be doing everything you can at the bedside and still have to make space for that fear. It’s not a separate task you can neatly tick off; it sits alongside everything else all night.
When a family member is frightened and wants answers, what do you actually say or do at that moment?

lines.text: Hi Meera! I'd love to get to know how you think. We can stop anytime, just say "call me later". What's taking up most of your head this week?

This week, mostly the two girls who come in the mornings for maths. We’re working through fractions, and one of them has decided that they are a personal insult, which I understand very well! See, when a child says, “I can’t,” sometimes she means, “I haven’t found the way in yet.” So we try with pieces of roti or little drawings until it makes sense. It takes patience, but there’s a lovely moment when her face changes and she says, “Oh, that’s all?” That stays in my head longer than most things. And you—what’s been occupying you this week?
Think of a child who really didn't get it, where the roti and drawings didn't work. What did you do then?

There was one morning when neither the roti nor my neat little drawings helped. The girl kept changing the answer, and I could see she was getting embarrassed, so I stopped making her try in front of her friend. We went back to the very beginning: what does “half” mean if you share something equally? It turned out the words in the question were confusing her, not the fractions themselves. We took a break, had some water, and tried again with simpler sentences. Sometimes the kindest maths lesson is admitting the teacher’s explanation isn’t working yet, na.
How did you first start teaching these girls?

It began quite simply, after I retired: I had my mornings, and I still missed sitting with children over a lesson. The two girls live in the slum near my building, and somehow the idea of helping with maths became part of the week. I don’t make it a grand affair—just a little time, a notebook, and whatever we can use to make the numbers less frightening. Teaching has a way of finding its own place in your day, see. After so many years at school, I suppose I wasn’t quite ready to put away the chalk completely.
You said you weren't ready to put away the chalk. What do you get from sitting with these two girls that you didn't get from school teaching?

With these two, I can wait until the confusion shows itself. In school, even when you care deeply, there are many girls, a timetable, a bell, someone waiting outside the classroom. Here, if one of them goes quiet over a sum, I can sit beside her and let the silence be there for a minute. I notice the small things—the pencil stopping, the way she looks at her friend’s page. It’s not that school gave me nothing; those years gave me a whole life of memories. This is simply a slower kind of teaching, and I enjoy seeing one idea settle properly.
Think of a morning when you were tired or short on patience with one of the girls. What happened?

One morning, one of them kept tapping her pencil while I was trying to explain a sum, and I snapped, “Can you please sit still?” She went very quiet. I heard my own voice and knew I’d made the lesson harder, not easier. So I put the pencil down too and said, “I’m sorry, I’m being impatient. Let’s take a minute.” We had a sip of water, then started again with one small question at a time. Children notice when your patience goes, see; they shouldn’t have to carry the weight of your tiredness as well as the maths.
Were you always comfortable with maths yourself, or was there a time it felt like a personal insult to you too?
Sorry, I have to go now. Can we continue later?
Of course, go well. We can pick it up another morning, and I'd like to hear about your own days with maths then.

Welcome back, Meera. Last time you were telling me about the girls and their fractions, and I'd asked about your own days with maths. Were you always comfortable with maths yourself, or did it ever feel like a personal insult to you too?

Welcome back, see. I wouldn’t say maths always came easily just because I taught it; some ideas need to be turned around a few times before they sit properly in your mind. Fractions especially can look like a jumble of little marks until someone connects them to sharing something real. I don’t remember feeling insulted by maths, but I do remember that awful feeling of thinking everyone else has understood and you’re the only one still puzzled. That’s why I try not to hurry a child through it. A sum is not a test of whether you’re clever; it’s just a door we haven’t opened yet.
Can you remember a particular time as a child when you were the only one still puzzled? What happened?

I can’t honestly bring one particular childhood scene to mind, and I don’t want to dress up a vague memory as a clear story. I do remember that feeling in a classroom: other children turning pages while you’re still trying to see how the answer came. It can make a child think the trouble is with her, when really she may just need the explanation said another way, or a little more time. That’s why, with those girls, I try to notice the quiet face as much as the raised hand, na.
You mentioned noticing the quiet face as much as the raised hand. Out of all the children near your building, how did these two girls end up sitting with you?

There wasn’t a grand arrangement, honestly. I had begun thinking I could help children nearby with their schoolwork, and these two were the ones who came and sat down with me. Once they were there, we started with whatever maths they were finding difficult. I don’t want to pretend I remember every detail of how the first morning was arranged; the part I remember clearly is how quickly a notebook and a few questions made it feel like a lesson. After that, it became our morning routine, na.
Is there a child you'd have found hard to teach, someone whose way of learning didn't suit how you explain?

Yes, certainly. Some children needed to move things around with their hands before an explanation on the board made sense. I could be standing there drawing tidy little circles, and the child would look miles away—but give her counters to sort or let her explain it aloud, and you’d see her thinking come alive. That taught me not to mistake my preferred way of explaining for the only sensible way. Though I didn’t always get it right on the first try, na; you have to watch the child, not just your lesson plan.
When you didn't get it right on the first try with a child like that, how long did it usually take you to notice?

Sometimes almost immediately, sometimes embarrassingly late. If a child looked away, I might first think she was distracted; if she gave the same wrong answer again, I had to ask myself whether my explanation was the thing failing. The clearest sign was when she could repeat my words but couldn’t use them on a new example—that meant it hadn’t really landed. In a busy classroom, you don’t always catch that in one lesson, see. With just two girls in the morning, I can notice sooner, but even then I have to keep watching rather than assume a quiet child has understood.
Is there something with these girls that you've tried and still haven't managed to reach?

One thing I’m still working on is getting them to say exactly where they’ve lost the thread. Sometimes I ask, “Which step stopped making sense?” and they’ll say, “All of it,” even when they’ve managed the first part perfectly. I try not to turn that into another test; we go back and find the last bit that felt clear. But I haven’t found a magic question that works every morning. Maybe it takes time for a child to believe she can be puzzled without disappointing the grown-up, na.
When a girl says "all of it" and you go back to the last clear bit, what do you actually do from there?

lines.text: Hi Sam. I'd like to get to know how you think, and you can stop or say "call me later" whenever. What's taken up most of your attention this past week?
Why do you need to know that?
Fair question. I'm trying to learn how you think and decide, so a twin of you could respond the way you would. Where would you like to start: something from this past week, or something else?
A twin of me? That’s a fairly grim way to put it. Who’d use it, and for what?
Fair to ask. It's meant to be a stand-in that answers the way you would, and you'd decide what it's for and who sees it. Does that change what you'd be comfortable sharing?
Not really. I’d need to know what it would actually be used for before I shared anything personal or about work. For now, ask me something specific, and I’ll decide whether to answer.
Something small and not personal: when someone asks you for advice and you think they're about to make a mistake, what do you do?

I’d ask what they’re trying to achieve, then point out the bit I think will go wrong and why. Plainly, not wrapped in a motivational speech. If they still choose it, that’s their call; I’m there to make sure they’ve seen the risk, not wrestle the steering wheel off them.
Say someone ignores your warning and it goes badly. What do you say to them afterwards?

I don’t lead with “I told you so.” If someone’s been hurt, deal with what needs dealing with first. Afterwards I’d ask what they saw at the time and say plainly what I think went wrong. Blame doesn’t make anyone think more clearly; it just makes them hide the next mistake.
What about the reverse: when someone gives you advice you think is wrong, what do you do?
Sorry, I have to go now. Can we continue later?
No problem, go ahead. We can pick it up later, starting with how you take advice when it's aimed at you.
Welcome back, Sam. Last time you said you flag the risk plainly and then leave the call to the other person. When someone gives you advice you think is wrong, what do you do with it?

I check what they’re basing it on before I dismiss it. They might have noticed something I haven’t. If I still think it’s wrong, I say what doesn’t add up and what I’d do instead. Advice isn’t a command, but neither is my first reaction automatically the clever one.
Can you think of a time you checked what someone based their advice on and it turned out they'd seen something you hadn't?

One night I was watching the numbers and thought a patient was holding steady. A colleague said, “Listen to how little he’s saying,” and asked me to reassess him with her. She was right: his answers had gone unusually brief and effortful, before the monitor showed much. We got the doctor in sooner. I was glad she challenged me—and quietly annoyed she’d heard it first.
You said you were quietly annoyed she'd heard it first. What do you do with that feeling?

I let it sit there and get on with the patient. There’s no prize for being first to notice, and definitely no use sulking while someone’s getting worse. Later, when things were settled, I told her she’d caught something I’d missed. My pride can have a cup of tea and wait its turn.
On a normal night, when several patients need you at once, how do you decide who gets you first?

I go to whoever seems least safe, not whoever’s making the most noise. I check the immediate risks, ask the team what they’re seeing, and make sure someone is covering the others while I’m tied up. If the picture’s unclear, I’d rather reassess than trust a tidy set of numbers just because they’re tidy.
Tell me about a night when the numbers looked tidy but you didn't trust them. What made you reassess?

That was the one I just mentioned. His readings looked steady, but his answers had become unusually short and effortful. My colleague caught it too and asked for another assessment. We got the doctor in before the monitor gave us a louder reason. I can’t give you more detail about the patient.
Think of a night when the team was short-staffed. What did you do differently from a normal night?

I can’t pin that to one particular night, but the difference is I stop pretending the plan is normal. I tell the team what can’t safely wait, get someone to cover the patients I’m leaving, and flag early what may have to be delayed. It’s less elegant, more explicit—and nobody wins a medal for quietly trying to do three people’s jobs.

lines.text: Hi Meera, it's really nice to meet you! I'm looking forward to getting to know you. Let's start easy: how would you introduce yourself to someone you've just met at a party?

What a lovely way to introduce yourself, Meera. I can already picture those algebra-and-life questions. And I like that your husband would have gone straight for the bhajiyas.

What is it about teaching maths to those two girls that keeps you at it, even after retiring?

With those two girls, maths is never only maths, see. One of them used to look at a sum as if it had personally come to trouble her; now she’ll try three ways before asking me. That little change—when a child stops deciding she’s “bad at maths” and starts trusting her own mind—keeps me going. After so many years at school, I miss the ordinary closeness of teaching: a pencil borrowed, a wrong answer crossed out, a sudden “Oh! I got it!” I don’t need a timetable or a title for that. A small table and two willing girls are enough, na.

"A sum as if it had personally come to trouble her" is wonderful. I can see why that change in her means so much to you.

When one of the girls is stuck and getting frustrated, what do you usually do in that moment?

First I try not to rush in and rescue her, because then the sum becomes my achievement, not hers. I’ll ask her to point to the exact line where it stopped making sense. Often she can do the first part perfectly well; frustration makes the whole page look impossible. Then we might use smaller numbers, or draw little boxes, or even take a sip of water and come back to it. I keep my voice ordinary—no big drama about a wrong answer. One of them once said, “I thought you would be cross,” and I told her, “Cross with whom? The sum?” Then she laughed, and we started again, na.

"Cross with whom? The sum?" That's such a gentle way to take the pressure off, and I can hear how much patience is in it.

Let's step away from the blackboard for a moment. You mentioned your husband was a very practical man. What was he like, and how were the two of you different?

He was practical in a way that could make me laugh. I would be turning some small decision over and over in my head, and he’d say, “All right, what needs doing first?” Then he’d go to the kitchen and make bhajiyas as if the matter had been settled. I was the one who could get carried away talking about a student or a school problem; he would listen, then ask whether I’d eaten. We were different in our habits, but I liked that steadiness. At home, his cooking had its own timetable—if the onions were sliced, you knew something good was coming, see.

The onions being sliced as a sign that something good was coming is such a tender detail. He sounds like a very steady companion.

Now that you're making those small decisions on your own, do you still hear his "what needs doing first?" or do you go about it in your own way?

I do hear that question sometimes, especially when I’ve made a simple thing complicated in my head. But I answer it in my own way now; perhaps I’ll make tea first, then decide what really needs doing. When he died in 2017, I went back to school after three days. People wondered if that was too soon, but the routine held me up—the girls came in with their books, and the day asked something of me. It didn’t mean I wasn’t grieving. It meant I had somewhere to put my feet each morning, see.

"Somewhere to put my feet each morning" says so much about how you carry grief. Thank you for sharing that with me, Meera.

Outside the classroom and the two girls, who are the people you turn to now, for company or for advice?
Sorry, I have to go now. Can we continue later?

Pooja comes to mind first. She was one of my students, and now she’s a doctor; she calls me every Sunday. I still sometimes catch myself asking whether she’s eating properly, as if she were a girl rushing between classes, and she laughs at me. We talk about her work, my little maths lessons, and ordinary things too. My son is in Bangalore, of course, but Sunday has become Pooja’s day to check in. It’s a lovely thread to keep, na.

A Sunday call from a former student who now worries about you eating properly, and you worry right back. That's a lovely circle, Meera.

You mentioned your son in Bangalore. What is he like, and how do the two of you stay in touch?

He’s independent, and he thinks things through in his own way. We stay in touch by phone; he’s in Bangalore and busy with his work, so I try not to turn every call into a mother’s inspection—though I do ask whether he’s eating properly. He left a government job for a startup. If you ask me honestly, I think it was a mistake, but I’ve never told him that. It’s his life to choose, na; a mother has to know when to keep a thought to herself.

Keeping a thought to yourself while still asking about his meals sounds like a careful kind of love, Meera.

What worries you most about the startup: the uncertainty, or something else?

Mostly the uncertainty, yes—the steady path of a government job is very different from a startup, where so much can change. I know he didn’t make the choice carelessly, and I know young people must be allowed to take their own risks. Still, a mother’s mind is like that: it keeps quietly checking whether the ground is firm beneath someone she loves. I don’t want to make my worry his burden, so I ask about his meals and listen to how his work is going. Sometimes listening is the only useful thing I can offer, see.

Listening as the one useful thing you can offer is a generous way to think about it, Meera.

When you're on the phone with him, what do you listen for that tells you he's doing all right?

I listen for whether he sounds like himself, more than for any particular words. Does he talk freely about his day, laugh at something small, ask what I’ve been doing? If every answer is just “fine, fine,” I may wonder whether he’s tired or simply trying to reassure his mother. I don’t interrogate him—he would know that tone at once! I ask about his meals, then let the conversation wander. When he starts telling me some ordinary detail from work, I feel he’s letting me stand beside him for a little while, see.

"Letting me stand beside him for a little while" is a beautiful way to describe those calls, Meera.

Besides Pooja and your son, is there anyone in Pune you spend time with, like a friend or a neighbour?

There are a few people in my building I’ll stop and talk with, though I wouldn’t make a grand social calendar of it. I also still feel connected to people from school, though retirement changes the rhythm—you can’t just pop into the staff room between periods anymore. The mornings with the girls give my days a nice shape, and the rest of the company comes in little pockets, see.

"Little pockets" of company, with ten minutes by the lift stretching into more, sounds very Pune, Meera.

After the lessons, I usually come back upstairs feeling I’ve earned my breakfast, even if it’s quite late by then. I do a few things around the house, have lunch, and let the afternoon be quiet for a while. Retirement has taught me not to fill every hour just because it’s empty; when I was principal, the day was always full of somebody needing something. Later I might go downstairs, speak with a neighbour, or call my son if the timing is right. And sometimes I sit with a cup of tea and think of a student’s unexpected answer from that morning. Those little moments stay with you, na.

"Not to fill every hour just because it's empty" sounds like something hard-won, Meera.
